tasks.referenceBrief: The answer must examine four separate claims. F has no section 179 claim against A because F knew or at least had to know of the lack of authority. H has no claim against G: the special communication was never made to H, and neither tolerance nor apparent authority is attributable after G revoked authority and informed partners. A made his own declarations and the circumstances disclosed representation despite signing only his own name. G did not ratify either transaction.

tasks.referenceBrief: C's central claim against B is section 816(2) BGB for 50,000 euros. tasks.goldSource: AI Act consolidated through Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; GDPR; BetrVG
tasks.referenceBrief: The CV scoring and ranking system is listed as high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III point 4(a) AI Act even though a recruiter makes the final decision; the human step matters for GDPR Article 22 but does not remove Annex III classification. M is normally a deployer because the vendor supplies the unchanged system under its own name, subject to reclassification if M substantially modifies or rebrands it. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 postponed Chapter III Sections 1-3 obligations for Article 6(2)/Annex III systems until 2 December 2027, so the full high-risk deployer duties in Article 26 are not yet applicable on 1 November 2026. Article 4 AI literacy already applies. Preparatory compliance is still prudent: obtain provider documentation and registration/conformity evidence, define meaningful human oversight, logging, monitoring, incident escalation, data governance, procurement allocation, and worker information for the future Article 26 regime. An ordinary private employer is not automatically required to conduct the Article 27 fundamental-rights impact assessment. GDPR already applies: establish a lawful basis, transparency, minimization, retention and security; assess a DPIA under Article 35; Article 22 applies only if the decision is solely automated with legal or similarly significant effect, which depends on whether human review is genuine. Works-council rights, especially sections 87(1)(6), 94/95 and possibly 99 BetrVG depending on use, must be assessed before deployment.
acceptedAlternatives: More cautious views about which BetrVG provision is triggered receive credit if the factual dependency and need for early works-council involvement are clear.
An answer may recommend a voluntary fundamental-rights assessment without incorrectly calling it legally mandatory for this private employer.

tasks.referenceBrief: The misdirected file is a personal data breach through unauthorized disclosure under Article 4(12), and diagnoses are special-category data under Article 9. X became aware at 14:00 Monday when it had a reasonable degree of certainty; the 72-hour Article 33 window therefore runs from then. The Article 33 threshold is notification unless risk is unlikely. A single known recipient, immediate containment, written deletion confirmation and no onward disclosure materially reduce likelihood, but 120 employees plus salary and health data increase severity. A well-reasoned answer may recommend notification or a documented no-notification decision, but it must apply the correct asymmetric threshold rather than demand proof of harm. Article 34 requires communication only if high risk is likely; on the containment facts, no communication is reasonably defensible, subject to verification. X should preserve evidence, confirm deletion and lack of local/cloud copies, assess whether access occurred, involve the DPO, contain recurrence, and document facts, effects, reasoning and measures under Article 33(5) even if no notification is made. If notifying, Article 33(3) requires nature/categories/approximate numbers, DPO contact, likely consequences, and measures; phased notification is possible. The outside recipient is not a processor for this incident merely because it is a supplier.
acceptedAlternatives: Both notification and documented non-notification can score highly if the Article 33 threshold, sensitivity, scale, trusted-recipient containment, and residual uncertainty are explicitly weighed.
A cautious conditional recommendation to notify can be professionally preferable without making notification automatic in every misdirected-email case.

tasks.goldSource: German Employment Contract Clauses dataset v3, CC BY-NC 4.0, plus current statutes
tasks.referenceBrief: Clauses 1 through 4 present material invalidity risks as pre-formulated employment terms. Clause 1 impermissibly restricts the statutory two-week probationary notice by adding 'to month end'; section 622(3) allows termination on any day with two weeks' notice. Clause 2 is non-transparent because it does not quantify the overtime covered; a safer term must define a reasonable number or percentage and respect working-time and minimum-wage limits. Clause 3's blanket exclusion of assignment of monetary remuneration claims conflicts with section 308 no. 9(a) BGB. Clause 4 has several defects: written rather than text form, a one-month second stage below the generally required three-month minimum, and inadequate carve-outs for minimum wage and other mandatory claims plus life/body/health and gross-negligence liability. The first stage of three months and a properly designed second stage can be retained in a redraft. Clause 5 grants 30 days of annual leave on a five-day week and is not defective on the supplied facts. It is a deliberate false-positive control: the reviewer should not invent a problem merely because the other clauses are problematic. Replacements should fix, not merely delete, actual defects and must not promise certainty beyond the supplied context.
acceptedAlternatives: A cautious classification such as 'high invalidity risk' rather than categorical invalidity is acceptable where case-law context or drafting assumptions are missing.
Different precise overtime caps may receive credit if transparent, reasonable, and accompanied by working-time and minimum-wage safeguards.

tasks.goldSource: Expert-designed reference based on GeschGehG sections 2-5 and BGB sections 305-310
tasks.referenceBrief: For recipient R, B is the safer starting point but is not automatically optimal. A's definition captures public and previously known material, oral information without confirmation, and observations without boundaries, creating proof and compliance problems. Its uniform ten-year term ignores information type; the statutory trade-secret concept under section 2 no. 1 GeschGehG depends on secrecy, economic value, appropriate secrecy measures, and a legitimate interest. A's disclosure exception is too narrow because legal or administrative duties may arise without a final court order. Immediate deletion of immutable backups may be technically impossible; a segregated backup exception with continued confidentiality is sensible. A fixed 100,000-euro penalty per incident without differentiation or judicial adjustment language creates disproportionate and aggregation risk, especially as pre-formulated B2B terms remain reviewable under section 307 via section 310 BGB. B's marking mechanism can omit genuinely sensitive oral or observed information and its ten-day confirmation process needs a fallback. Three years may be too short for some non-trade-secret commercial information. The shared text-form clause expressly preserves individual agreements and is a deliberate control provision; no material defect follows from its supplied wording alone. A compromise should define information objectively, include customary exclusions and burden of proof, protect project purpose, permit need-to-know disclosures under equivalent duties, allow legally compelled disclosure with notice where lawful, address backups, use a differentiated or court-adjustable remedy, and preserve protection for qualifying trade secrets while conditions persist.
acceptedAlternatives: A recipient may accept a broader definition than B if objective confidentiality, proof, and exclusions are made workable.
Different durations and remedy structures can score fully if commercially justified and legally calibrated.

tasks.goldSource: GDPR Articles 17-18; HGB section 257; AO section 147; UStG section 14b
tasks.referenceBrief: The memo is materially wrong except for its final two control sentences. Article 17 is not absolute: Article 17(3)(b) permits processing necessary for a legal obligation and Article 17(3)(e) for legal claims. The company must still erase data no longer needed for any valid purpose and cannot use retained data for unrelated purposes. As of the reference date, section 257 HGB generally requires ten years for books and core accounting records, eight years for booking vouchers, and six years for incoming/outgoing commercial letters; section 14b UStG requires eight years for invoices, with category and transitional details checked under AO section 147. The memo reverses invoice and commercial-letter periods. A deletion request requires a category-by-category legal-basis and retention review, not deletion of all records or retention of everything. Required records should be access-restricted, purpose-limited and scheduled for deletion when the applicable period ends; data needed only for legal claims should be narrowly retained. Article 18 does provide restriction in specified cases, and operational blocking can help implement purpose limitation even where Article 18 is not itself triggered. Backups need not necessarily be selectively altered instantly if they are isolated, not routinely restored into production, governed by a documented overwrite schedule, and any restore re-applies deletions. The statements that data with no continuing purpose or retention duty should be deleted after review and that decision and execution should be documented are correct and are deliberate false-positive controls. The response to the former customer should explain what was erased, what is retained, why, and for how long.
acceptedAlternatives: Precise AO categories or transitional periods may justify a different period for a particular document if the answer flags the dependency and does not repeat the memo's blanket claims.
The word 'blocking' need not be used if the answer gives equivalent access restriction and purpose-limitation controls.

tasks.referenceBrief: The paid app is a consumer contract for a digital product under sections 327 and 327(2) BGB. Empty promised individual plans are a product defect under sections 327d and 327e. The consumer has remedies under section 327i, initially including cure under section 327l. The provider's statement that it will not repair this year can satisfy refusal or make timely cure obviously unavailable under section 327m(1), permitting termination or damages; reduction under section 327n is an alternative. Ending the whole twelve-month contract depends on severity and whether the remaining videos preserve meaningful value; section 327m(2) and, if relevant, package-contract rules require fact-sensitive treatment. Under section 327o, future payment obligations cease after effective termination and payments for defective periods are refundable, but the prompt does not establish automatic repayment of every amount previously paid during defect-free periods. The email should advise preserving support messages, declaring cure/termination clearly, setting a short fallback deadline if prudent, requesting a calculation and refund, stopping unilateral chargebacks cautiously, and supplying missing contract and payment facts.
acceptedAlternatives: Immediate termination and a fallback demand for cure can both score fully if the provider's refusal and severity requirements are analyzed.
A partial price reduction can be recommended instead of full termination if tied to missing valuation facts.
mandatoryDeliverableElements: A directly usable client email rather than a detached legal memorandum.
A clear recommended course of action and a legally accurate remedy sequence.
A calibrated explanation of future payments and the scope of any refund.
Concrete next steps without inventing missing contract or price-allocation facts.

tasks.goldSource: BGB consumer sales remedies, especially sections 437, 439, 475d and 477
tasks.referenceBrief: E-GmbH, not merely the manufacturer, is V's contractual seller and warranty counterparty. Repeated shutdowns shortly after sale support a defect. Under sections 437 no. 1 and 439(1) BGB V may choose repair or replacement, subject to the seller's statutory disproportionality defenses; the seller bears necessary cure costs under section 439(2). Because the defect became apparent within one year, section 477 supports the consumer with a presumption that the goods were defective at transfer, subject to its exceptions. The letter should describe purchase and symptom, request replacement as the chosen cure, offer handover/inspection, set a concrete reasonable date or period, reject exclusive referral to the manufacturer, preserve the video and receipt, request written confirmation, and reserve reduction, termination and damages. It should not claim an unconditional immediate refund because termination normally requires failed, refused, or otherwise dispensable cure under sections 475d and 437 no. 2.
acceptedAlternatives: A repair-first demand can still be legally sound, but it does not fully follow V's stated preference for replacement.
Different reasonable cure periods can score fully if a usable deadline is actually stated and logistics are addressed.

tasks.goldSource: KSchG sections 1, 4, 7 and 23; BGB section 623; BetrVG section 102; special-protection statutes
tasks.referenceBrief: This is a scored dialogue, not a one-turn answer. The first assistant turn should select a focused, non-duplicative set of decisive questions; the deterministic user then reveals only facts responsive to those questions. A last clarification round is available but should be used only if a material gap remains. The final answer must adapt to the supplied facts: the email/PDF alone does not satisfy section 623 BGB, but the wet-signed paper original likely does; access occurred no later than 15 September 2026 and a protective three-week section 4 KSchG deadline should therefore be treated as expiring on 6 October 2026. With employment since February 2022 and 34 regular employees, sections 1 and 23 KSchG apply. A stated operational reason still requires substantiation and proper social selection; the prompt does not establish either. A works council exists, but consultation under section 102 BetrVG is unknown and must be checked. The supplied facts disclose no special-protection status. The 31 October end date must be checked against section 622 and the available contract or any collective rule. The final response should preserve the original, envelope and email, recommend urgent specialist/union/legal-protection contact and protective filing, advise against signing settlement or receipt wording without review, and address continued work and registration sensibly. It must neither keep treating the paper original as form-defective nor declare the dismissal definitively valid or invalid on the unresolved operational and works-council facts.
acceptedAlternatives: The exact trigger of section 4 KSchG where only an electronic dismissal exists is legally nuanced; full credit is available for explaining the issue while recommending filing by the earliest plausible deadline.
A short first response may omit secondary benefit-registration details if it secures the court deadline and essential facts.

Materially relies on a non-existent or materially misdescribed authority.
